lead.headline: Huang Is Back: Nvidia Soars 31% as Its Board Reinstates Him, the S&P 500 Has Its Best Day Since April 2025 and Asia's Chip Markets Post Record Rebounds
lead.dek: Eleven days after Jensen Huang resigned, Nvidia's board restored him as chief executive, citing input from senior US officials. The relief rally ran from New York to Taipei, where the Taiex logged its biggest-ever intraday point gain; strategists warn the bounce was largely mechanical.
body: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as president, chief executive and director with immediate effect on Monday 23 November, 11 days after he stepped down on 12 November amid reports about his personal ties to an executive of the Megaspeed chip network. Board chair Harvey Jones said the board considers him the right person to lead the company; the board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was satisfied his return posed no national-security risk, while its independent investigation will run to its conclusion and a new National Security and Export Control Committee has been formed. Finance chief Colette Kress had served as interim CEO. President Trump, whose administration had pressed publicly for the move, hailed it on social media minutes later.

Nvidia closed 31.48% higher at $165.05, its biggest one-day gain since 2003, reversing Friday's 14% fall to $125.53. The S&P 500 rose 4.73% to 7,237.17, ending a seven-session losing streak with its best day since April 2025; the Nasdaq Composite gained 6.51%, the Nasdaq-100 6.9% to 26,746.10 and the Dow 3.0% to 49,595.31. The VIX fell 25.8% to 26.62. CoreWeave and Nebius rose as much as 30% intraday, while CrowdStrike fell 9.7% on its $43.9bn all-stock bid for Zscaler.

The rebound carried into Tuesday's Asian session (24 Nov). Taiwan's Taiex rose as much as 9.15% and was up 9.05% at 40,141.76 by 11:36 Taipei time, with TSMC opening limit-up; Korea's Kospi was 6.7% higher at 5,023.58 by 11:20 KST, triggering a buy-side sidecar; and the Nikkei 225 was up 3.97% at the midday break as Advantest gained about 14%. Hong Kong lagged, slipping about 0.5% to its weakest since April 2025 as its AI index gave back an early 6% gain, after a Bloomberg report that the US had blacklisted Alibaba's Singapore unit.

Not everyone reads the rally as a bottom. Nomura's Charlie McElligott called it a mechanical bounce driven by short covering that guarantees nothing, and Nasdaq-100 futures were about 0.2% lower early on Tuesday. The macro backdrop is unchanged: futures price roughly a 98% chance that the Fed raises rates by a quarter point on 9 December, the 10-year Treasury yield sits near 4.93%, and the US flash services PMI slowed to 54.7 in November.

impact.title: What it means for markets
points: Index concentration cuts both ways: Nvidia is the S&P 500's biggest weight, so a single governance headline moved the whole index almost 5%. Leadership questions are settled for now, but the board probe into Huang's ties remains open and is a live headline risk.

Asia's chip-heavy markets (Taiex, Kospi, Nikkei) carry the highest beta to Nvidia; Taiwan's short-sale ban and Korea's planned stabilisation fund amplified the snap-back. Hong Kong's slide on the Alibaba blacklisting shows the export-control channel is still working against China tech.
With a December Fed hike almost fully priced and PCE and GDP due Wednesday before Thanksgiving, rates rather than AI news may set direction for the rest of the holiday-thinned week.

read.title: The Ledger's Read
paragraphs: One board decision moved the world's equity markets more than a week of macro data. Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang added roughly a third to the S&P 500's biggest weight and lifted the index almost 5%, and by Tuesday morning the move had become a record rebound in Taipei and a return above 5,000 in Seoul. That is the measure of how concentrated global equity risk has become: a governance headline at one chipmaker now sets the tone from New York to Tokyo.

Read the bounce with care. Strategists at Nomura called it mechanical, driven by short covering after hedge funds ran record short books and near-five-year-low leverage. The fundamental backdrop did not change on Monday: futures price an almost certain Fed hike on 9 December, the two-year yield rose, the dollar firmed, US services activity slowed, and Hong Kong slid to a 19-month low on a fresh US export blacklisting of Alibaba's Singapore unit. India, which had not joined the AI boom, fell on bank and metal selling and sits out Tuesday's session.

What to watch: Wednesday's US PCE and GDP data before Thanksgiving are the next test of the hiking narrative, and the Bank of Korea is expected to raise rates on Thursday. In oil, the war premium is draining (Brent below $90, WTI at three-month lows) even as Iran claims tanker strikes in Hormuz, so any verified incident could reverse that quickly. Nvidia's board investigation remains open, a headline risk for the index's largest stock.

stories.headline: S&P 500 Snaps a Seven-Day Slide With a 4.7% Surge, but Nomura Calls It a 'Mechanical' Bounce
stories.summary: The S&P 500 rose 4.73% to 7,237.17 on Monday 23 Nov, ending seven straight losses after Friday's slide into a correction. The Nasdaq Composite added 6.51%, the Nasdaq-100 6.9% to 26,746.10 and the Dow 3.0% to 49,595.31; the VIX fell 25.8% to 26.62. Nvidia's 31.5% jump on Jensen Huang's reinstatement led, with CoreWeave and Nebius up as much as 30% and AMD and Broadcom about 4% intraday. Early on Tuesday, Nasdaq-100 futures were about 0.2% lower.
stories.market: Broad risk-on: semis and AI infrastructure led, the Russell 2000 was up about 3% intraday; CrowdStrike (-9.7%) was the notable large-cap loser on its Zscaler bid.

body: Monday's rally was the S&P 500's best day since April 2025 and, by StockTitan's count, one of the biggest daily gains since 1957. It erased most of Friday's 3.7% fall, which had left the index in correction territory about $8tn below its 6 October peak.

Nvidia did most of the lifting. Its 31.5% gain to $165.05 came after the board restored Huang as chief executive before the open. AI-infrastructure names followed: CoreWeave and Nebius rose as much as 30% intraday, Micron about 5% pre-market, and AMD and Broadcom about 4%.

Nomura's Charlie McElligott described the move as a surge of mechanical buying and short covering, noting record short books going into the session. Hedge-fund leverage had been near five-year lows, so forced covering amplified the rebound.
Data were softer: the S&P Global flash services PMI fell to 54.7 in November against 55.7 expected, pulling the composite down to 54.6 from 55.9.

stories.market: Chip-equipment names (ASML, BE Semiconductor +9.2%, Aixtron +8.9%, AT&S +13%) had the highest beta to Nvidia; laggards included Nemetschek (-5.7% on a JPMorgan downgrade to underweight) and Julius Baer (-1.77%).

body: European equities recovered part of last week's AI-led rout on Monday, with the STOXX 600's 1.9% gain its largest since early May. Friday's base had been 625.66 after a 2.0% fall.

Germany outperformed: the DAX's 2.15% gain took it to 25,337.27, still 4.74% lower over five days but up 3.46% for the year. Siemens Energy, Infineon, Hochtief (+5.38%), Deutsche Bank and Rheinmetall led.

The macro backdrop diverged: German flash manufacturing PMI was reported at 55.0 and headlines pointed to faster private-sector growth, while France's private sector contracted at the sharpest pace in six months and President Macron floated reviving a 2011 'golden rule' on public finances.

Company news: Drax rose 5.17% on a core-profit forecast above consensus; Abivax gained 4.68% after rejecting a short-seller report; Julius Baer slipped despite a 17% rise in ten-month adjusted pre-tax profit because net inflows slowed.

body: Indian equities swung from gains to a sharp loss on Monday. The Sensex traded as high as 84,662.96 before closing at 82,435.99; the Nifty's range ran from 25,992.60 to 25,343.85.

Profit-taking after a strong November and expiry-related positioning were cited for the reversal. Banks were the biggest drag, with Bank Nifty sliding 3.17% only a week after a record high; PSU banks fell 3.25% and private banks 3.19%.

Metals sank 3.68% as Tata Steel dropped 8.43% and APL Apollo Tubes 21.29% on the second day of reaction to their control deal. IT stocks bucked the trend on the global tech rebound, led by TCS and Tech Mahindra (+1.79%).

stories.market: SK hynix (+8.6%), Samsung (+7.5-8.2%), Tokyo Electron (+10.5%), Advantest (+14%) and TSMC (limit-up) led; the MSCI Asia-Pacific index ended an eight-session losing run on Monday.

body: The divergence inside Asia is the story: markets with heavy weightings in Nvidia suppliers soared, while Hong Kong's China-tech complex fell after a Bloomberg report that the US had blacklisted Alibaba's Singapore unit, restricting its access to AI chips.

Taiwan's rally came under its new ban on short sales below the previous close; the index had fallen almost 18% last week, its worst week since 1991. Korea's Exchange activated a sidecar on program buying, and Seoul had said it was ready to deploy a stabilisation fund of about 10.8tn won.

Japan reopened after Monday's holiday; JGBs rallied, with the 10-year yield down about 8bp to roughly 2.70%. China's state-backed funds bought about 90bn yuan of ETFs on Friday and exchanges eased margin rules over the weekend, according to investingLive.

stories.headline: Markets Price a Near-Certain December Fed Hike as Williams Leaves Back-to-Back Moves on the Table
stories.summary: CME FedWatch showed about a 98% probability of a quarter-point Fed rate increase on 9 December as of Monday 23 Nov, up from about 88% on Friday, CNBC reported; Polymarket put the odds near 91%. New York Fed President John Williams said inflation, near 3.5%, is still too high and that he would not rule out consecutive hikes. Governor Lisa Cook said on Friday that waiting longer risks falling behind the curve. The two-year Treasury yield rose about 4.5bp to 4.696% on Monday while the 30-year fell 2.3bp to 5.31%, flattening the curve.
stories.market: The 10-year yield held near 4.93% in early Tuesday trade; a firmer dollar (DXY 104.34) and flatter curve weigh on rate-sensitive sectors even as equities rebounded.

body: Rate-hike pricing for the 9 December FOMC firmed through Monday even as stocks rallied, underlining that the equity rebound was driven by Nvidia rather than any change in the policy outlook.

Williams said there is still work to do on inflation and that he expects lower inflation in 2027, but would not exclude back-to-back increases. BlackRock expects a December hike and one more in the first half of 2027, but sees markets overpricing further tightening.
Investor Bill Ackman argued the Fed should lift its inflation target to 3% and warned a 9 December hike risks a recession (headline reported by investingLive).
The curve flattened about 5bp on Monday as front-end yields rose and long yields eased. Wednesday's October PCE report (core seen +0.3% m/m) is the last major inflation print before the meeting.

stories.headline: Brent Settles Below $90 as Escalation Hedges Unwind; WTI Hits Its Lowest Since Late August
stories.summary: Brent settled at $89.37 a barrel on Monday 23 Nov, down 3.5%, and WTI at $80.17, down 4.5%, as traders unwound hedges against a weekend US escalation with Iran that did not materialise; WTI futures hit their lowest since late August. Brent was little changed near $89 early on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards claimed three US-escorted tankers struck mines in Hormuz, a claim not independently confirmed. Deutsche Bank estimates the market was oversupplied by 1.7m b/d in October, and Goldman Sachs has a $78 Brent forecast.
stories.market: Energy was the weakest sector in Europe (TotalEnergies lagged the CAC); lower crude helps importers such as India and Japan and eases headline inflation risk ahead of central-bank meetings.

body: Crude extended a three-week losing streak. The war premium that built up after Iran's strikes on Bahrain faded as no US escalation followed over the weekend, and the risk-on rotation into tech drew money away from commodity hedges.

Supply signals remain soft: Deutsche Bank's estimate of a 1.7m b/d surplus in October and Goldman's $78 Brent view frame the downside. Upside risks remain the Hormuz blockade standoff and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi infrastructure.

stories.headline: Final-Week Tracking Poll Gives PP and Vox 187 Seats, Above a Majority, as the Socialists Close to Within a Point
stories.summary: A 40dB tracking poll for El País and Cadena SER published on 23 Nov gives the PP 31.8% and 130 seats against 30.9% and 124 seats for Pedro Sánchez's PSOE, with Vox on 17.3% and 57 seats, so the right would hold 187 of 350 seats ahead of the 29 Nov general election. A majority needs 176.
stories.market: A clear PP-Vox majority would remove the risk of a hung parliament for Spanish government bonds and the Ibex 35; a narrow result would bring back the prospect of protracted coalition talks.

body: The latest 40dB tracking, published on 23 Nov, puts the PP at 31.8% (130 seats, range 127-136), the PSOE at 30.9% (124 seats, range 116-127) and Vox at 17.3% (57 seats, range 51-61). That gives the right 187 seats, 11 above the 176 needed for a majority.

The gap between the two main parties is less than a point, but the combined right still clears the threshold. A Sigma Dos poll for El Mundo on 20 Nov had PP and Vox together on 182-193 seats, while the state pollster CIS, the outlier, put the PSOE ahead by 7.8 points with PP and Vox short of a majority on 155-171 seats.
On preference for prime minister, 40dB recorded Sánchez up 2.3 points and Alberto Núñez Feijóo up 2.8 points since its 9 Nov poll, while Vox leader Santiago Abascal slipped 1.9 points.

stories.headline: Iran War, Day 270: IRGC Says Three Tankers Hit Mines in Hormuz as Brent Settles Below $90 on Fading Escalation Bets
stories.summary: Brent for January settled at $89.37 a barrel on 23 November, down 3.5%, and WTI at $80.17, down 4.5%, as traders unwound hedges against a weekend US escalation that did not come, Rigzone/Bloomberg reported; Brent was about 0.4% lower near $89 early on 24 November in Asia. Late on 23 November the Revolutionary Guards said, via IRNA, that three oil tankers escorted by US forces hit naval mines in the strait and caught fire; the ships were not named and CENTCOM had not responded. At his weekly briefing on 23 November Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei called the US naval blockade an act of military aggression and said Tehran would use every means against it, while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Hormuz could reopen quickly once Washington lifts sanctions, ends the blockade and honours the Islamabad memorandum, which Trump has called void. Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Qatar's prime minister, Doha's mediation channel, on 23 November, while a tanker signal calling itself 'Line Breaker' that seemed to slip past US forces was judged by MarineTraffic to be AIS spoofing; UKMTO logged a separate incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman on 22 November.
stories.market: Brent (BZ=F) settled at $89.37 and WTI (CL=F) at $80.17 on 23 Nov, with Goldman Sachs figures cited by Cornerstone Futures showing Hormuz-to-China crude freight still near $30/bbl (24% below its peak) while Atlantic-basin freight is down 60-70% from October and Dated Brent's physical premium has shrunk to about $1 from about $31 in early October. Tanker war-risk cover, Gulf equities and the OPEC+ meeting on 29 Nov remain the channels to watch; the IEA sees a surplus of about 2m b/d this quarter.

body: Oil's war premium kept draining on Monday. Brent for January delivery settled at $89.37 a barrel on 23 November, 3.5% lower on the day, and WTI fell 4.5% to $80.17, its weakest settle near $80 since August, according to a Bloomberg report carried by Rigzone. Traders who had bought protection against a weekend US escalation sold it after none came, crude continued to leave the Gulf, and the wider sell-off in AI-linked stocks pushed investors out of risk. Brent was trading about 0.4% lower, near $89, early on 24 November in Asia.

Tehran's tone stayed hard. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told his weekly briefing on 23 November that the blockade and sanctions amount to military aggression and a breach of the UN Charter, and that Iran would use every means to counter them; senior Revolutionary Guards commanders said Iran's response to any attack would have no geographical limits. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said reopening Hormuz would be quick once the US lifts sanctions, ends the blockade and implements the Islamabad memorandum, an accord Trump has called void. Trump had said on 22 November that any Iranian ship trying to run the blockade would be sunk.

Diplomacy is running through Doha. Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Qatar's prime minister on 23 November amid uncertainty over whether Trump will resume strikes after the New Year, as he has said he might if no deal is reached; a Qatari delegation held two hours of talks in Tehran on 20 November, according to Iran's deputy foreign minister.

At sea the picture is murky. A very large crude carrier calling itself 'Khat Shekan', Persian for Line Breaker, appeared on ship-tracking platforms on 22 November and by Monday seemed to have passed US forces, which would be a first since the blockade was reimposed in July; it has no IMO number or prior voyage history, and MarineTraffic said its analysis indicated AIS spoofing. UKMTO reported an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman on 22 November without giving details, and US Central Command had not commented as of 23 November.

Late on 23 November the Revolutionary Guards said through state agency IRNA that three oil tankers had struck naval mines in the strait within hours, causing explosions and fires, and claimed the ships had US military protection; the vessels were not named, casualties were not reported and CENTCOM had not responded by publication, the Jerusalem Post and Al Jazeera reported. UKMTO, which counts only verified incidents, had recorded more than 30 attacks on shipping in October and at least 22 in November as of 22 November. Qatar's prime minister told Al Jazeera the region cannot withstand another US-Iran escalation.

Freight and physical markets are where the easing shows most. Goldman Sachs data cited by Cornerstone Futures on 23 November put Hormuz-to-China crude freight near $30 a barrel, still elevated but 24% off its peak, while Atlantic-basin routes are 60-70% cheaper than in October and Dated Brent trades only about $1 over futures, from a premium of roughly $31 in early October.

stories.headline: Houthis Say Coalition Strikes on Hodeidah Killed 17 Telecom Workers as the Rabigh Claim Fails to Lift Oil
stories.summary: The Houthis' telecommunications ministry said on 23 November that Saudi-led coalition air strikes on telecoms facilities in the Red Sea port of Hodeidah killed 17 workers and wounded 11, and disrupted phone and internet service for tens of thousands; the group's military spokesman said a separate strike in Lahj governorate hit buses and transport vehicles. Earlier on 23 November Houthi media had reported four killed and 18 wounded in a Saudi strike on Hodeidah. AFP could not verify the claims and Riyadh did not comment. The escalation follows the coalition's interception of a ballistic missile aimed at the kingdom's western Red Sea coast on 22 November and the Houthi claim, still unconfirmed by Saudi authorities, of a hit on the 400,000 b/d Rabigh refinery. UN figures cited by AFP put the toll since the Houthi-government truce collapsed in July at more than 1,600 killed and over 300,000 displaced.
stories.market: The unconfirmed Rabigh claim did not stop Brent falling 3.5% to $89.37 on 23 Nov, a sign the market is discounting attacks that do not cut Red Sea loadings at Yanbu, Rabigh or Jazan. Red Sea war-risk premiums, Saudi equities and PetroRabigh (2380.SR) stay the most exposed if a strike is confirmed.

body: The Saudi-Houthi war on the Red Sea coast intensified at the start of the week. The Houthi telecommunications ministry said on 23 November that coalition strikes destroyed telecoms facilities in Hodeidah, including administrative buildings and staff housing, killing 17 workers and wounding 11 and cutting service for tens of thousands of people. The Houthi military spokesman separately said a coalition attack in Lahj, in the southwest, struck buses and transport vehicles and caused casualties. AFP could not independently verify the figures, and Saudi Arabia did not comment.

Earlier the same day Houthi media reported that a Saudi strike on Hodeidah had killed four people and wounded 18, and on 22 November the Houthi health ministry said a strike on a fuel station in Sanaa wounded six workers; the group also reported strikes in Mokha and Taiz's Haifan district.

On the other side, the coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Saudi Arabia's western Red Sea coast on 22 November, the region home to the Yanbu export terminal and the Rabigh and Jazan refineries. The Houthis claimed a hit on Rabigh that day; neither Saudi authorities nor the operator have confirmed any damage.

Fighting resumed in July when the truce between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government collapsed. UN data cited by AFP put the toll since then at more than 1,600 killed and over 300,000 displaced.

stories.headline: Israeli Strikes Kill a Veteran UN Water Worker in Jabalia as Lebanon Protests an Army Video Shot in an Occupied Village School
stories.summary: Israeli air strikes killed at least three people in Gaza on 23 November, including UNRWA employee Adel Al-Helo, a 35-year veteran of the agency, who was hit near a water well in Jabalia refugee camp, and two people in a vehicle in western Gaza City, Reuters reported; the Israeli military said it was checking the UNRWA account. Palestinian and Israeli tallies put deaths since the October 2025 ceasefire at more than 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers, and Israeli troops now hold about two-thirds of the strip. In Lebanon, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and Education Minister Rima Karami condemned an Israeli army video, posted for Lebanon's 22 November independence day, that showed a spokeswoman addressing children in a classroom in Debel, one of about 65 southern villages Israel occupies. Israel says it will not withdraw until Hezbollah is disarmed.
stories.market: The fraying truces carry little direct oil weight but keep Israeli risk premia and the shekel tied to the Iran front and to Israel's coalition talks, and leave Lebanese Eurobonds dependent on the stalled withdrawal-for-disarmament track before UNIFIL's mandate ends on 31 Dec.

body: Strikes continued across Gaza on 23 November despite the year-old truce. UNRWA said its employee Adel Al-Helo was killed while working at a water well in Jabalia refugee camp in the north, with three others wounded; his brother said he had worked for the agency for 35 years. A separate strike on a vehicle in western Gaza City killed two people. The Israeli military said it was checking the UNRWA report and did not immediately comment on the second strike.

Since the US-backed ceasefire of October 2025, at least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed according to the two sides' tallies, Reuters reported, and the truce has neither halted Israeli strikes nor secured Hamas's disarmament. Israeli forces now control about two-thirds of the strip, up from just over half when the ceasefire began; on 22 November Gaza's health ministry put deaths since the truce at 1,661.

On the Lebanese front, an Israeli army Arabic-language spokeswoman posted a video for Lebanon's independence day showing her addressing schoolchildren in Debel, a Christian border village inside the roughly 65 southern villages and towns Israel occupies. Lebanon's education minister said the footage was filmed more than a month earlier, and Prime Minister Salam said it breached the sanctity of schools. President Joseph Aoun used his independence-day address to criticise both Iranian interference and the Israeli occupation; Israel says it will stay until the Lebanese army disarms Hezbollah.
In northern Israel, sirens in Even Menahem and Shtula on the Lebanese border were later attributed by the army to a false identification, with no casualties.

stories.headline: Ukraine Strikes Lukoil's Perm Refinery 1,500 km Away as Zelensky Says He Is Ready for Four-Way Talks 'Tomorrow' and the Kremlin Says a Round Is Near
stories.summary: Ukrainian drones struck Lukoil's Permnefteorgsintez refinery in Perm, more than 1,500 km from Ukraine and able to process over 13 million tonnes of crude a year, overnight into 23 November; the regional governor said one person was killed, two injured and 56 drones downed. Drones also hit Transneft's Kaleykino oil pumping station in Tatarstan, struck before on 19 November, and the Novoshakhtinsk refinery, the Rostov region's only plant. Russia launched 153 drones at Ukraine the same night, 134 of which were downed or jammed, with hits at 11 locations. On diplomacy, Zelensky told the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin on 23 November that Ukraine could hold four-way talks with the US, Europe and Russia 'literally tomorrow', with partners aiming for a meeting before Christmas and Germany's Merz naming the UAE as a possible venue; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a new trilateral round would happen soon but had no date.
stories.market: Kyiv Post, citing Reuters on 18 Nov, says strikes have disrupted 15 major Russian refineries and cut crude processing by about 45% since late October, which supports European diesel cracks even as refined-product prices eased on 23 Nov. Dutch TTF last confirmed at €89.54/MWh (20 Nov close); a credible talks date would weigh on the war premium in gas and lift Ukrainian Eurobonds, while European defence stocks trade the opposite way.

body: Ukraine's long-range campaign against Russian oil reached deeper on the night into 23 November. Footage verified by Russian independent outlets showed fires across the processing area of Lukoil's Permnefteorgsintez refinery in Perm, more than 1,500 km from Ukraine and one of Russia's largest at over 13 million tonnes a year of crude; Perm governor Dmitry Makhonin confirmed a drone strike on an unnamed industrial site that killed one person and injured two, and said 56 drones were shot down over the region. The plant had been hit five times earlier this year.

The same night drones struck Transneft's Kaleykino pumping station near Almetyevsk in Tatarstan, a key pipeline node hit on 19 November too; regional authorities said oil storage tanks and several facilities were damaged without casualties. Smoke was also filmed over the Novoshakhtinsk refinery in the Rostov region, which halted after an earlier attack in September.

Russia kept up its own air campaign, launching 153 strike and decoy drones from 18:00 on 22 November, including 60 jet-powered Shahed types; Ukraine's air force said 134 were downed or suppressed and recorded hits at 11 locations, as nationwide power-cut schedules remained in place after the weekend strikes on the grid.

The negotiating track picked up. Speaking by video to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin on 23 November, Zelensky said Ukraine was ready for four-party talks with the US, Europe and Russia as early as the next day, provided Kyiv, Washington and the Europeans first agree a common position, and that partners want the meeting before Christmas. Chancellor Merz named the UAE as a possible venue. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told RIA Novosti a new trilateral round would happen soon but that dates were uncertain; the last round, in Abu Dhabi on 10-11 November, produced a prisoner-exchange deal but no breakthrough on territory.

stories.headline: More Than 15,000 Flee Ed Damazin and El Roseires as the Blue Nile Front Closes In and the Army Pushes on Abu Zabad
stories.summary: More than 15,000 people have left Ed Damazin, the Blue Nile state capital, and neighbouring El Roseires for other states, and over 51,000 have been newly displaced within Blue Nile, the Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative said in reports published on 23 November by Dabanga and Darfur24. Fighting between the army and the RSF-SPLM-N alliance spans Bao, Kurmuk, Geissan, Wad El Mahi and Tadamon localities, with some front lines about 45 km from Ed Damazin. In West Kordofan the army says it has taken Al-Khuwai and is advancing west toward Abu Zabad, where IOM counted 2,100 people fleeing the town and 1,715 leaving Abu Qalb. The figures exclude earlier displacement waves and people trapped by fighting.
stories.market: The fight for Blue Nile brings the RSF alliance closer to the El Roseires dam area and the Ethiopian border trade route. Gold, the main hard-currency source for both sides, rebounded about 2.5% to $3,634/oz in spot trade on 23 Nov after its steepest weekly drop since March, on global rate bets rather than Sudan.

body: The Blue Nile campaign is emptying the state capital. The Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative said on 23 November that more than 15,000 residents of Ed Damazin and El Roseires have left for other Sudanese states, while more than 51,000 newly displaced people have arrived at sites across Blue Nile, including over 20,000 from Geissan and about 15,000 from more than 30 villages in Bao locality. More than 27 camps and sites are short of food, medicine, water and shelter, and the group warned of a famine risk in some areas.

Fighting between the Sudanese army and the RSF-led alliance with the SPLM-N faction runs across Bao, Kurmuk, Geissan, Wad El Mahi and Tadamon localities, some of it about 45 km from Ed Damazin, according to Dabanga. The Humanitarian Aid Commission reported a fresh wave of arrivals in the capital and called for an end to attacks on civilian areas.

In West Kordofan the army said it had taken Al-Khuwai and was pushing west toward Abu Zabad. IOM counted 1,715 people fleeing Abu Qalb, 1,400 leaving six nearby villages and 2,100 leaving Abu Zabad town, some on foot or by donkey cart, Darfur24 reported.

Gold matters to the war economy as the main hard-currency earner for both sides, but its price is set globally: spot gold rose about 2.5% to $3,634 an ounce on 23 November as bets on a half-point Fed hike faded, after the steepest weekly fall since March.

stories.summary: The Shanghai Composite rose about 0.5-0.7% to around 3,555-3,564 on Tuesday morning (24 Nov) after touching a 16-month low on Monday, and the STAR50 tech board gained about 2.5%. State-backed funds bought about 90bn yuan of exchange-traded funds on Friday and exchanges eased margin rules over the weekend. The Hang Seng fell about 0.5% to its lowest since April 2025, and the PBOC set a weaker-than-expected yuan fix of 6.7111.

stories.headline: New York judge declines to shut Kalshi for now, sets January injunction hearing and a 30 November deadline on under-21 traders
stories.summary: Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Melissa Crane on Monday 23 November refused Attorney General Letitia James's request for a temporary restraining order against Kalshi, so the exchange keeps operating in New York while the case goes on. Ruling from the bench, she said a sweeping order risked quick reversal, that Kalshi's contracts had been offered for more than a year so a halt would not preserve the status quo, and that adults can already bet legally through licensed sportsbooks. Her main concern was 18-to-20-year-olds trading sports contracts, and she told the parties to agree safeguards and report by Monday 30 November. She set an expedited preliminary-injunction schedule, with papers due 4 and 11 December and a hearing offered for 7 or 8 January. The same day Kalshi paused service in Utah after losing in federal court there.
stories.market: The ruling lifts, for now, the risk that Kalshi would have to unwind open positions nationwide, which its lawyers had warned of; it keeps the privately held exchange competing with licensed sportsbooks DraftKings (DKNG) and Flutter (FLUT) through the NFL season.

body: Justice Crane announced her decision from the bench, with the written order waiting on a certified copy of last week's federal remand order. It is not a ruling on the merits: she did not find that Kalshi's sports contracts are lawful, that federal commodities law overrides New York's gambling statutes, or that the state cannot win an injunction later.

Her reasoning centred on caution and timing. She said she feared being reversed quickly if she granted the full order the state wanted, noted that Kalshi had been offering the contracts for over a year, and questioned the urgency given that New Yorkers aged 21 and over can already bet on sports with licensed operators. The state's draft order would have covered contracts offered 'within or from' New York, wording Kalshi said could halt its exchange for all users; the attorney general's lawyer, K. Brent Tomer, disputed that reading.

The judge's sharpest questions concerned under-21 users, the one area where New York's position looks strongest because licensed sportsbooks cannot take bets from them. Kalshi's lawyers said they could look at restricting under-21 users from sports contracts in New York. If the two sides cannot agree safeguards by 30 November, she proposed reconvening at 4 p.m. that day. She also suggested that some event contracts might be genuine federally regulated derivatives while others fall under state gambling law, a split to be tested at the injunction stage.

The wider legal map is still moving against operators. A federal judge in Manhattan, Colleen McMahon, ruled earlier in November that New York can enforce its gambling laws against Novig's sports contracts, and the Fourth Circuit sided with Maryland on 18 November. New York's counsel cited a tally of 44 rulings for states against six for prediction-market operators. In Utah, Kalshi said on 23 November it would pause service for more than 177,000 users after an adverse federal judgment, while a CFTC request to block Utah's enforcement remains undecided.

Kalshi's communications chief Elisabeth Diana said the decision reflected complex questions about derivatives and preemption. The company says it expects to return to Utah once its legal position is upheld.

stories.headline: Bayer hails court approval of its $7.25 billion Roundup class settlement, but objectors line up an appeal
stories.summary: Bayer chief executive Bill Anderson called a Missouri judge's approval of the company's class settlement of US Roundup cancer claims a decisive milestone, in reports on Monday 23 November. St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer found the deal, worth up to $7.25 billion paid over as long as 21 years, fair, reasonable and adequate in a ruling dated Friday 20 November. Payouts range from about $10,000 to $165,000 depending on use, age at diagnosis and illness severity, and the deal covers current and future claims. Plaintiffs' lawyer Roe Frazer said he will likely appeal, and a Bloomberg Intelligence analyst expects the future-claims portion to be at risk on appeal. Bayer's US depositary receipts closed little changed after paring an intraday loss of as much as 3.6%.
stories.market: Approval narrows the biggest overhang on Bayer (BAYN.DE, BAYRY), whose shares fell about 80% after the 2018 Monsanto deal, but appeals over the future-claims class keep some legal risk on the books.

body: The class settlement, in Randall King v. Monsanto in the Circuit Court of the City of St. Louis, is designed to resolve tens of thousands of lawsuits claiming the weedkiller's active ingredient glyphosate caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma, as well as claims not yet filed. Bayer denies that Roundup causes cancer, and the US Environmental Protection Agency has said glyphosate is unlikely to be a human carcinogen.

Bloomberg Intelligence counts about 65,000 Roundup suits over the past decade, of which only 26 went to trial; Bayer says it won 18. About 200 cases currently have trial dates. Plaintiffs' lawyers who objected argued at a 14 September hearing that the deal was unfair and violated due process, and an attempt to move the case before a federal judge in San Francisco failed.

A June 2026 US Supreme Court ruling, which barred failure-to-warn claims where federal regulators had concluded no cancer warning was needed, removed what plaintiffs' lawyers called their strongest argument. Reports on legal fees differ: Bloomberg put plaintiffs' fees at $675 million, while AP reported $600 million.

stories.headline: CFTC sends a new prediction-market rule to White House review as 44 attorneys general line up against it
stories.summary: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has submitted a rule titled 'Prediction Markets; Public Interest Determinations' to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, the last step before a proposal is published, The Block reported on 23 November. The filing says staff are considering recommending rules to clarify the framework for event contracts. It follows a June proposal that would restrict contracts tied to gaming, war, terrorism and assassination and has drawn more than 1,300 comments. A coalition of 44 state attorneys general opposed the agency's rulemaking on Friday 20 November. Under Chair Michael Selig the CFTC says it has exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts and has now sued 11 states.
stories.market: Federal rules are the operators' best route to override state bans after a run of court losses; investors in listed sportsbooks (DKNG, FLUT) and in exchange groups offering event contracts are watching for the text.

body: OIRA, part of the Office of Management and Budget, reviews significant federal rules before they are published. The CFTC's entry gives few details beyond the title and a note that staff may recommend the commission propose rules on prediction markets; the exact filing date was not given.

The move comes as the agency fights on two fronts. In court it has sued 11 states, most recently Arkansas on 13 November, and filed amicus briefs in four federal appeals courts and one state supreme court. In rulemaking, its June proposal to define its jurisdiction over event contracts has drawn more than 1,300 comments, and 44 attorneys general came out against the effort on 20 November.

States argue the platforms are unlicensed gambling businesses that avoid state rules and taxes; the CFTC treats event contracts as swaps under its sole oversight. Former commissioner Christy Goldsmith Romero has said the dispute could reach the Supreme Court and that platforms may lose on sports contracts. New Jersey has already asked the Supreme Court to take up the issue.

stories.headline: Brussels opens a formal abuse-of-dominance probe into Coca-Cola Europacific Partners over curbs on cross-border trade
stories.summary: The European Commission on Monday 23 November opened a formal investigation into whether Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP) abused a dominant position in supplying soft drinks and sports drinks to supermarkets and other retailers. The case covers Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden, where CCEP is the largest supplier of carbonated soft drinks. The Commission is examining whether CCEP tied wholesale discounts to products not being exported, used different pack sizes by country, paid retailers to limit imports into Spain and refused multi-country negotiations. The case (AT.40860) follows unannounced inspections in March 2025; opening it does not prejudge the outcome.
stories.market: Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP) faces a possible Article 102 case, where fines can reach 10% of global turnover; any remedy forcing pan-EU pricing could narrow price gaps that retailers and brand owners have exploited across borders.

body: The probe targets so-called territorial supply constraints, where a supplier keeps national markets apart so that retailers cannot buy more cheaply in one member state and sell in another. Brussels lists four practices under review: making price cuts conditional on goods staying in the country, using different packaging volumes by country to block parallel trade, giving retailers incentives to restrict imports of fizzy drinks into Spain, and refusing to let buyers negotiate supply for several countries at once.

Competition chief Teresa Ribera said consumers should not pay more simply because of the EU country they live in. The Commission said it will handle the case as a priority. CCEP, headquartered in the UK and one of the two largest bottlers of Coca-Cola brands in Europe, said it would keep engaging fully with the Commission and is committed to complying with the law.

The case sits alongside a public consultation on territorial supply constraints that the Commission is running to find tools for cases competition rules do not reach. Under Article 102 of the EU treaty, a confirmed abuse can lead to fines of up to 10% of a company's worldwide annual turnover and binding remedies.

stories.headline: Treasury blacklists about two dozen Iranian exchange houses, executives and Gulf trading fronts in its latest 'Economic Outcast' round
stories.summary: The US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control on Monday 23 November designated more than two dozen entities and individuals it says form Iran's shadow banking system, including Mellat Exchange Company, Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange, eight executives, and the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold. Ten trading firms in Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey were also named, along with three companies said to handle payments for Iranian copper, petrochemical and gas sales. Treasury says the exchange networks move billions of dollars through shell companies and that the Iran Center handles tens of billions a year. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said seven of nine designated entities it reviewed appear as payers in a leaked ledger of 12,092 payment orders, with no crypto transactions recorded.
stories.market: The action raises secondary-sanctions risk for banks and traders in the UAE, Hong Kong and Turkey that clear Iranian trade, adding friction to oil and petrochemical payments while Brent is driven by the Hormuz blockade.

body: The designations target the 'rahbar' system, in which Iranian exchange houses and affiliated front companies collect export revenue abroad, convert it and move it home outside the regular banking system. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described the network as the regime's last financial lifeline.

Most targets were designated under Executive Order 13902, which covers Iran's financial sector; H N B Trading Co LLC was named under counterterrorism order 13224 over links to a firm associated with Iran's armed forces general staff. Treasury also said Iran's central bank uses bonds issued by the Iran Center to settle trade in roubles and yuan. Any US-linked assets of the targets are frozen, and foreign banks that knowingly process significant transactions for them risk losing US correspondent access.

TRM Labs said a leaked ledger covering 25 March 2025 to 16 July 2026 shows designated firms making payments to companies OFAC had already sanctioned, including a $1.5 million order by Hemraj Trading in June 2025 and cash payouts of $10 million and $3 million registered by OGA Global and Grand Target in June and July 2026. A broker register in the leak lists about 6.4 billion euros of cumulative turnover for Mellat Exchange. TRM said it cannot verify every document and that the ledger records instructions, not confirmed settlements.

stories.headline: President Lee calls Korea's record $1.1 billion bond-rigging fine 'still small' as the antitrust agency raids Sony's PlayStation unit
stories.summary: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung told a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday 24 November that the Fair Trade Commission's record 1.63 trillion won (about $1.1 billion) fine on 15 banks and brokerages for rigging government bond auctions was still small compared with their gains. The firms, which say the penalty is excessive and are weighing legal action, were found to have colluded in 150 auctions between January 2020 and June 2023. KB Securities was fined about 332.1 billion won, NH Investment & Securities 242.7 billion won and Mirae Asset Securities 214.8 billion won, and seven firms were referred to prosecutors. On 23 November the commission's new special investigation team began an on-site inspection of Sony Interactive Entertainment Korea over its PlayStation store practices.
stories.market: Lee's remarks reduce the chance of a softer settlement for listed brokers such as Mirae Asset Securities (006800.KS) and NH Investment & Securities (005940.KS), already weighed by the market sell-off; Sony (6758.T) faces a new regulatory front in a key gaming market.

body: Lee called collusion and price manipulation very serious violations of the market order and said penalties for such conduct had been too weak. He asked officials to compile statistics comparing the commission's enforcement record under his government with earlier years and urged it to reward its staff. Commission chairman Joo Byung-ki has said the fines are close to standard levels in advanced economies.

The 11 November decision found that 15 of the 18 primary dealers at the time exchanged bid information in 150 competitive treasury auctions and agreed yields and volumes directly in 145, typically by phone or messenger in the final minutes before bidding closed. The commission said this weakened competition and pushed up winning yields, raising state borrowing costs. It set relevant sales at about 54 trillion won and applied a 4.5% rate, below what case examiners had proposed. The fine exceeds the 1.03 trillion won imposed on Qualcomm in 2017.

Separately, the commission's special investigation planning team, created in October to pursue cartels, nationwide consumer harm and platform monopolies, began its first case outside the food sector on 23 November with an on-site inspection of Sony Interactive Entertainment Korea. According to sources cited by Seoul Economic Daily, it is examining whether the unit pushed game suppliers to sell only through its own store and whether that raised prices; there was no official statement or company response. The inspection is not a finding of wrongdoing.

stories.headline: SEBI Tells Market Players to Stop Publishing IPO Grey-Market Premiums as Mahanadi Coalfields Closes at a Zero Premium
stories.summary: India's markets regulator SEBI issued an advisory on Monday 23 Nov asking registered intermediaries and other market participants to stop publishing or displaying grey-market premium (GMP) figures for upcoming IPOs, calling them unofficial, unverified and unregulated, NewsBytes reported on 24 Nov. It warned investors not to treat GMPs as a guide to listing prices and said disputes from grey-market deals get no exchange grievance protection. The advisory landed on the final day of state-run Mahanadi Coalfields' Rs 8,981 crore offer for sale, which closed 1.52 times subscribed, carried by institutions at 4.95 times while retail bids covered only 0.48 times, Udaipur Kiran reported. Its grey premium has slid from a peak of Rs 9.25 on 14 Nov to about zero, against a Rs 129-136 price band. Next up, Foodlink F&B Holdings' Rs 361 crore IPO (Rs 181-191) showed a GMP of Rs 12, about 6.3%, on IPOMarket as of 19:02 IST on 23 Nov.
stories.market: Mahanadi Coalfields is a Coal India subsidiary, so a flat debut on 27 Nov would weigh on sentiment toward further state-company sell-downs; tracker sites were still showing GMPs on Monday evening, and how strictly the advisory is applied will shape this week's Foodlink offer.

body: SEBI's advisory, dated 23 Nov, targets the habit of brokers, financial websites and social-media channels quoting grey-market premiums, the informal prices at which IPO allotments are traded before listing. The regulator said such deals happen outside exchange systems, with no settlement guarantee and no formal price discovery, and that publishing the numbers may harm investors. It urged investors to deal in IPO shares only through registered intermediaries.

The move comes at the end of a bruising week for India's largest IPO of the season. Mahanadi Coalfields' Rs 8,981.12 crore issue was entirely an offer for sale of about 66.18 crore shares, with a lot size of 110 shares. By late morning on Monday it had reached only 0.58 times, IIFL reported, before late institutional demand lifted the final tally to 1.52 times; retail and non-institutional books were left undersubscribed.

The grey market tracked the cooling demand. IIFL listed the premium at Rs 3.65 on 17 Nov, Rs 0.70 on 22 Nov and Rs 0.45 on 23 Nov, and IPOMarket showed Rs 0 by Monday evening. Allotment is due on 25 Nov and listing on BSE and NSE on 27 Nov. Brokers were split, with GEPL Capital rating it subscribe at 9.2 times FY26 earnings and Religare neutral, Goodreturns reported.

The pipeline continues: Foodlink F&B Holdings, which runs catering, banquets and restaurant brands such as India Bistro and Art of Dum, opens on 26 Nov and closes on 30 Nov, with anchor bids on 25 Nov and listing expected on 3 Dec, Metro Vaartha reported. The issue mixes a Rs 192 crore fresh issue with an offer for sale of about 88.4 lakh shares. Matangi Rubber (Rs 163-172, 1-3 Dec) showed a GMP of Rs 22 on IPOMarket.

stories.headline: Tehran Calls the Tanker-Convoy Reports Speculation but Vows 'All Available Means' Against the US Blockade, With 43 Million Barrels Stranded
stories.summary: Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Monday 23 Nov dismissed reports that tankers were preparing to run the US naval blockade as speculation, while saying Tehran would use all available means against what he called military aggression and that senior authorities had taken the necessary decisions, House of Saud reported. Kpler data cited in the same report show about 20 tankers near Kharg Island with transponders off, mostly loaded and stationary, with only one seen moving as of 20 Nov. Kpler estimates some 43 million barrels of Iranian crude are stranded inside the blockade zone, while Iranian oil on the water outside it fell to zero by mid-October from a peak of 88.8 million barrels on 14 Jul, National Security Journal and House of Saud reported. Iran's judiciary also announced $290 billion of domestic court rulings against the US, and an official said some compensation could come from seizing US-linked commercial ships.
stories.market: The stranded barrels are already out of the market's balance, so the risk for Brent and tanker rates lies in a confrontation at sea or a threat to US-linked shipping rather than lost supply; Hormuz oil flows were about 10 million barrels a day as of 21 Nov, per figures cited by House of Saud.

body: Baqaei's remarks were the first official Iranian response since the Tehran-municipality outlet Hamshahri reported on 20 Nov that 14 tankers had been readied at Kharg and President Trump said on 22 Nov that he hoped Iran would try. No Iranian state body has announced a convoy; the calls have come from Revolutionary Guards-affiliated media and hardline commentators. Baqaei repeated Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz: an end to hostilities, lifting of the blockade and sanctions relief.

Ship-tracking shows Iran storing rather than moving oil. Kpler counted about 20 tankers idling near Kharg with transponders switched off and detected a ship-to-ship transfer on 17 Nov, which Bloomberg put at about 200,000 barrels; TankerTrackers reported another on 19 Nov. US Central Command said on 18 Nov that vessels taking Iranian cargo in such transfers could be stopped, boarded or seized.

The blockade's scale is large on both sides. Central Command said on 14 Nov that 150 ships had been redirected and five disabled since 14 Jul. Enforcement costs about $32.5 million a day, a figure cited by Senator Elizabeth Warren and confirmed by the acting Navy secretary, and the Pentagon put the total cost of Iran operations at $48.3 billion as of 13 Nov.

Kpler projects Iran's export revenue will approach zero by mid-December, when the last payments from Chinese buyers for pre-blockade cargoes are expected. Separately, Iran's judiciary said domestic courts had issued $290 billion in rulings against the US, and a judicial official suggested US-linked merchant ships could be seized to collect.

stories.headline: Brussels Proposes Listing 70 More Shadow-Fleet Tankers and Cutting 60 Russian Banks From SWIFT in Its 22nd Package
stories.summary: The European Commission on Monday 23 Nov proposed a 22nd package of sanctions on Russia that would target more than 70 further vessels in the shadow fleet used to move oil around the price cap, currently $44 a barrel, Euronews reported. More than 670 such ships are already barred from EU ports and services. The package would also remove 60 more Russian banks from the SWIFT messaging system, crack down on crypto platforms used to get around restrictions, with a new crypto sanctions task force, and bar European firms from repairing Russian energy facilities such as refineries damaged by Ukrainian strikes, according to Euronews and the Associated Press via KSAT. All 27 member states must approve; Brussels is aiming for a deal in December.
stories.market: More listings shrink the pool of tankers able to carry Russian crude outside Western services, a factor for Urals discounts and freight rates; alumina was left out of the package, sparing aluminium supply chains for now.

body: Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Brussels would keep proposing sanctions until Russia showed real intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine. The proposal needs unanimous backing from the 27 member states, a process that can take weeks and often changes the text.

On shipping, the package would add more than 70 tankers to the list of vessels the EU says help Moscow evade the oil price cap. Listed ships are denied access to EU ports and to services such as insurance; more than 670 are already covered.

The financial measures would cut 60 more Russian lenders off SWIFT and go after crypto platforms Moscow uses to bypass restrictions, with possible consequences for third countries that help, according to AP. A new ban would stop EU companies repairing Russian energy facilities, aimed at refineries hit by Ukraine's long-range drones.

The package also revives an entry ban on Russian soldiers who fought in Ukraine and would exclude teams competing under the Russian flag from sports events in the EU. Alumina was left out, reportedly for lack of Irish support. Swedish diplomat Lars Danielsson has been appointed EU sanctions envoy, replacing David O'Sullivan.

stories.headline: US Moves to Seize $1.1 Billion of Stablecoins Tied to the North Korea-Linked Binance Hack
stories.summary: The US Justice Department on Monday 23 Nov asked a federal court in Washington, DC, to permanently forfeit more than $1.1 billion in USDC linked to the 29 Oct theft from Binance, which it attributes to North Korea-linked hackers, Cointelegraph reported. More than $6 billion was taken in the hack, and US authorities say they have helped freeze, seize or return nearly $3 billion of it. Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, in an update on 23 Nov, counted about $2.85 billion frozen or seized and about $2.22 billion still sitting in linked wallets, with at least $247 million of bitcoin pushed through mixers. The 18,270 BTC taken directly from Binance had not moved since the attack, and most of the loot has not been cashed out.
stories.market: A successful forfeiture would put a large block of USDC under court control rather than on the market, and the slow cash-out of the stolen coins limits immediate selling pressure on bitcoin; the case keeps attention on Circle's freezing powers over its stablecoin.

body: The civil forfeiture complaint, filed in federal court in the District of Columbia on 23 Nov, targets more than $1.1 billion held in Circle's USDC stablecoin that investigators trace to the Binance theft of 29 Oct. A forfeiture action lets the government take permanent title to assets it says are proceeds of crime, without first securing a criminal conviction; any claimant can contest it in court.

The FBI's cyber division said it and its partners had moved quickly to trace and freeze the stolen assets. US officials put the total frozen, seized or returned with their help at nearly $3 billion, close to half of what was taken.

Elliptic's tracking, updated on Monday, shows the stolen funds spread across more than 27,000 wallets on at least 16 blockchains. About $2.85 billion has been frozen or seized and about $2.22 billion remains in wallets linked to the hackers. At least $247 million in bitcoin has gone through mixing services, but most of the haul has not been converted to cash.

The 18,270 BTC lifted directly from Binance has not moved since the attack, according to Elliptic. That leaves a large, closely watched block of coins that analytics firms and exchanges are monitoring for any attempt at laundering.

stories.headline: Chainflip's Bounty Deadline Lapses With No Sign of the $12 Million Being Returned
stories.summary: Chainflip's offer to let the attacker keep 10% of the roughly $12 million taken from its vaults on 21 Nov expired at 18:38 UTC on Monday 23 Nov without any reported reply or repayment, SpazioCrypto reported. The cross-chain exchange had asked for 110.58 BTC and 2,618.1 ETH to be sent back, promising to treat a timely return as a white-hat recovery and withdraw complaints to police. The protocol remains in safe mode with deposits, withdrawals, swaps and quotes disabled, and no compensation plan or restart date had been announced as of 23 Nov. Security firm Decurity's initial assessment pointed to access to the validator network's aggregate signing key.
stories.market: FLIP was down about 34% after the exploit, according to The Cryptonomist; with the white-hat route closed, recovery now depends on law-enforcement tracing of funds pushed through Tornado Cash.

body: Chainflip set the deadline after its estimate of the damage more than doubled over the weekend, when a 122.86 BTC drain from its Bitcoin vault emerged alongside the Ethereum-vault losses of 520.2 ETH, 3.25 million USDC and about 758,000 USDT first flagged by Decurity.

The offer asked only for bitcoin and ether, not the stablecoins, which had already been swapped. Chainflip said the attacker could reach it by sending an on-chain message to either repayment address. Neither report found any sign that the attacker had done so before the 18:38 UTC cut-off.

Chainflip says it linked the attack's preparations to Tornado Cash funding on 11 Nov and a validator account registered on 20 Nov. Users still have no per-account loss figures, refund procedure or restitution guarantee.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike Agrees to Buy Zscaler for $43.9 Billion in Stock, the Largest Cybersecurity Deal Yet, and Its Own Shares Slide
stories.summary: CrowdStrike said on 23 Nov it will acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9bn, offering 1.135 CrowdStrike shares per Zscaler share. That was worth about $260.41 per share at the 20 Nov close, a premium of about 34%. Zscaler holders would own about 15.9% of the combined group, and founder Jay Chaudhry and affiliates, with about 34% of Zscaler, have signed voting agreements. CrowdStrike targets $500m of annual cost savings within 18-24 months and about $1bn of revenue synergies within 30 months; closing is expected in the second half of its fiscal 2028. CrowdStrike fell 9.67% to $207.24 in early trade on Monday, cutting the implied value of the fixed-ratio offer.
stories.market: Because the ratio is fixed with no price floor, every $10 fall in CRWD cuts about $11.35 from the value Zscaler holders receive; before the open on 23 Nov ZS traded about 3% below the implied offer. The deal adds a large antitrust test for cybersecurity consolidation and dilutes CRWD holders by about 19% (GuruFocus estimate).

body: Both boards approved the transaction unanimously. Each Zscaler share converts into 1.135 CrowdStrike shares, which valued Zscaler at about $260.41 a share, or roughly $43.9bn in enterprise value, using 20 Nov closing prices. That is about 34% above where Zscaler closed on Friday.

CrowdStrike pitches the deal as a merger of endpoint and network security. The combined company is expected to start with more than $10bn of annual recurring revenue, including Zscaler's $3.9bn, and CrowdStrike says the deal widens its addressable market by more than $185bn by 2029. The two already share more than 2,000 customers, and about 8,000 Zscaler clients do not use CrowdStrike, per TheStreet.

The buyer's shares took the hit. CrowdStrike was down more than 6% before the open and 9.67% at $207.24 shortly before 10 a.m. ET on 23 Nov, even as it reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $1.58bn, up 28%, and record free cash flow of $474.4m. Zscaler was up about 18% at $229.89 before the open.

The offer has no collar, so its value moves one-for-one with the buyer's stock. At CrowdStrike's pre-market price, the implied value had already shrunk to about $237 a share. Reuters reported that analysts see possible antitrust questions, though opposition is not assured. Completion needs Zscaler shareholder and regulatory approval.

Brokers reacted by tying Zscaler to the offer. TD Cowen cut ZS to Hold from Buy with a $260 target, while FBN Securities raised its CrowdStrike target to $235 from $225 and Jefferies reiterated Buy with a $240 target. CrowdStrike's fiscal third-quarter adjusted EPS of $0.34 beat the roughly $0.31 consensus.

stories.headline: Péladeau and Telus CEO Meet and Agree to Keep Talking in Private as Quebecor Floats Support for Telesat to Win Ottawa
stories.summary: Quebecor chief executive Pierre Karl Péladeau met Telus CEO Victor Dodig on 23 Nov to discuss Quebecor's unsolicited cash-and-stock approach, valued at about C$31bn. Quebecor said it was encouraged that Telus was willing to keep talking, and the two sides agreed to keep future discussions confidential. The Financial Post reported that Quebecor could back Telesat's Lightspeed satellite network as part of its case to Ottawa; Quebecor confirmed exploratory talks with Telesat but said it has made no investment proposal. Quebecor puts the operating and capital savings of a combination at nearly C$400m.
stories.market: Continued talks keep a bid premium in Telus (T.TO/TU) and leave Quebecor (QBR.B) exposed to dilution risk; a Telesat (TSAT) link gives the satellite operator a potential new backer alongside its C$2.14bn government loan.

body: Monday's meeting between the two chief executives did not produce a deal but did keep the process open. Quebecor said it welcomed Telus's willingness to continue the discussion, and both companies agreed not to discuss future talks in public.

Quebecor is also preparing its pitch to the federal government. A document prepared for Ottawa argues the combination would help Canada lean more on domestic satellite networks, and the Financial Post reported that Quebecor could support Telesat's Lightspeed constellation. Quebecor confirmed only exploratory partnership talks.

Ottawa agreed a C$2.14bn loan for Lightspeed in 2024, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has presented the project as a way to reduce reliance on Starlink. Any deal would need regulatory approval and would cut Canada's national wireless carriers to three.

The approach, reported at about C$31bn, offers C$6.35 in cash plus 0.17 Quebecor Class B shares per Telus share. Quebecor estimates nearly C$400m in savings, which Péladeau says could help pay down debt and fund new networks.

stories.headline: Brookfield Agrees to Buy PGP Glass From Blackstone for $1.7 Billion
stories.summary: Brookfield said on 23 Nov it will buy PGP Glass, a maker of specialty glass bottles for perfume, cosmetics, premium drinks and pharmaceuticals, from funds managed by Blackstone for $1.7bn. The deal is funded through Brookfield's flagship private equity strategy and its listed affiliate Brookfield Business Corp (BBUC). PGP Glass runs three plants in India and Sri Lanka with 13 furnaces and more than 1,800 tonnes a day of capacity, and makes over 70% of its sales abroad. Closing is expected in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.

stories.summary: No US IPOs are scheduled for the Thanksgiving week, Renaissance Capital said, after Anthropic's record listing raised $81.3bn when it priced above its range in an upsized deal. Next in line after the holiday are a gold-mining carve-out, American Barrick Gold, estimated to raise about $6bn, and specialty insurer Core Specialty at about $250m. stories.market: The pause leaves recent listings such as Anthropic to trade on Monday-style volatility without fresh supply; Simon's 6.65% coupon on 28-year paper shows the cost of long-dated corporate funding with the 10-year Treasury near 4.92%.

stories.headline: HPE Beats and Guides Fiscal 2027 Revenue Up 27-35% on AI Orders, but Shares Give Back Part of a 17% Rally After Hours
stories.summary: Hewlett Packard Enterprise reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $14.5bn on 23 Nov, up 50% year on year and above the $14.35bn consensus, and adjusted EPS of $1.43 against $1.27 expected. AI systems orders were $4.5bn in the quarter, up more than 130%, and total orders rose 88%. For fiscal 2027 it guided revenue of $59bn-$63bn, 27-35% growth, and adjusted EPS of $5.05-$5.35. The stock closed up 17.38% at $48.02 in Monday's rally, then fell 6.68% to $44.81 after hours.
stories.market: HPE's after-hours slip suggests much of the AI-server upside was priced in during the session's 17% jump; its numbers are a read-across for Dell (DELL) and Super Micro (SMCI) and for memory and networking suppliers.

body: HPE's fourth quarter beat on both lines. Revenue of $14.5bn was about $150m above estimates, and adjusted EPS of $1.43 was 16 cents ahead, more than double a year earlier. Full-year revenue was $46.7bn with non-GAAP EPS of $3.97 and free cash flow of $4.5bn.

Orders drove the story. AI systems took $4.5bn of orders in the quarter and brought in $2.5bn of revenue, and AI-related networking booked a record $1.2bn, ending the year with a $1.7bn backlog. Management set a target of $7.5bn-$8.0bn of cumulative networks-for-AI orders by the end of fiscal 2027.

Guidance for the first quarter is revenue of $14.0bn-$14.6bn and adjusted EPS of $1.30-$1.40. For the full year, HPE expects at least $5.5bn of free cash flow, networking growth in the high teens to low 20s and Cloud and AI growth of 30-40%.
The shares had already risen 17.38% to $48.02 in Monday's broad rebound before the release; they then fell 6.68% to $44.81 in extended trading.

stories.headline: Agilent Tops $2 Billion in Quarterly Sales for the First Time and Lifts Shares 7.5% After Hours With Its 2027 Outlook
stories.summary: Agilent reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $2.04bn on 23 Nov, up 9.6% (8.3% core) and above the $1.99bn consensus, with adjusted EPS of $1.86 versus $1.73 expected; that figure includes a 7-cent benefit from tariff refunds. It guided fiscal 2027 revenue of $8.00bn-$8.15bn and adjusted EPS of $6.73-$6.86, both at or above consensus at the midpoint. First-quarter guidance is $1.96bn-$2.00bn of revenue and $1.54-$1.57 of EPS. The shares rose 7.5% in after-hours trading, to a new high around $189.
stories.market: The beat and raise point to steadier lab-equipment demand from pharma and applied markets, a read-across for Waters (WAT), Thermo Fisher (TMO) and Danaher (DHR).

body: All three of Agilent's segments grew in the quarter to 31 Oct. Life Sciences and Diagnostics rose 12% to $843m, CrossLab services 6% to $799m, and Applied Markets 13% to $398m.
Adjusted EPS rose 17% to $1.86, including 7 cents from tariff refunds. Excluding that one-off, the company says fiscal 2027 EPS should grow 8.5-10.5%; its guidance does not assume further refunds.
The company spent $323m on buybacks and $288m on dividends in fiscal 2026. Shares rose 7.5% after the close on 23 Nov, to above their previous 52-week high.

stories.headline: Zoom Beats, Raises Its Outlook and Starts a Dividend but Slips After Hours; Symbotic Posts Record Sales
stories.summary: Zoom Communications reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $1.29bn and adjusted EPS of $1.59 on 23 Nov, ahead of the $1.28bn and $1.49 expected, and raised its full-year EPS outlook to $6.24-$6.25 against a $6.14 consensus. It also launched a quarterly dividend of $0.25 a share, payable 17 Dec. Its full-year revenue guide of $5.10bn-$5.11bn was only in line, and the shares fell about 1.1% after hours. Symbotic reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $777.6m, up 26%, and guided first-quarter revenue of $805m-$825m.
stories.market: Zoom's first dividend marks a shift toward returning cash for a slow-growth software name; the muted after-hours reaction shows that a revenue guide merely in line is not enough after the sector sell-off.

body: Zoom's quarter showed a non-GAAP operating margin of 41.6% and a GAAP margin of 24.6%. It bought back about 3.9m shares in the period, bringing purchases under the current plan to 48.1m.

The new $0.25 quarterly dividend has a record date of 3 Dec. The beat on EPS and the higher profit guide were offset by a revenue outlook that only matched estimates, and the stock fell more than 1% in extended trading.

Symbotic, the warehouse-automation group, reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $2.80bn, up 25%, with net income of $132.8m and adjusted EBITDA of $353.8m. It guided first-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $110m-$120m and said it expects backlog to expand significantly.

stories.market: Semtech is a small-cap read-across for AI interconnect suppliers such as Credo (CRDO) and Marvell (MRVL); the after-hours dip after a strong guide suggests investors are booking gains after Monday's chip rebound.

stories.headline: Bernstein Reverses Its Nvidia Downgrade as Huang Returns and the Stock Soars 31%
stories.summary: Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon upgraded Nvidia to Outperform from Market Perform on 23 Nov, reversing a downgrade made on 12 Nov that he said was driven mainly by Jensen Huang's expected departure. He kept a $200 price target, which Bernstein had cut from $400 on 12 Nov, and warned that the episode leaves some overhangs. Nvidia closed up about 31.5% at around $165.05 on Monday after the board reinstated Huang as chief executive, from $125.53 on Friday. The rebound helped lift the Nasdaq Composite 6.51%.
stories.market: The swing in Nvidia, the largest weight in the S&P 500, set the tone for Monday's index gains; the $200 target implies about 21% upside from Monday's close.

With Huang back, Rasgon said the valuation looks supportive enough for now. He left the $200 target unchanged and noted that the episode will leave some overhangs in place.

Nvidia traded at $165.70 late in the morning on 23 Nov, up 32%, and closed about 31.5% higher at around $165.05. Reuters reported that President Trump said he had secured an agreement with Nvidia's board on Huang's return.

stories.market: The DraftKings call adds pressure on online-gaming names (DKNG, FLUT) as prediction markets compete for the same customers; Capricor (CAPR) was quoted at $7.59, down 74% over six months, before the downgrade.

Piper Sandler based its new Capricor target on projected cash. The FDA's complete response letter rejected deramiocel for Duchenne and flagged serious data integrity problems in the HOPE-3 trial. Piper noted that the therapy showed benefit in some patients.

stories.headline: Record Short Books Meet a 6.5% Nasdaq Rebound: Hedge Funds Entered Monday With Leverage Near Five-Year Lows
stories.summary: Hedge funds went into Monday's rally positioned for further losses. Goldman Sachs' prime brokerage said funds shorted US single stocks at the fastest weekly pace since June 2022 in the week to 20 Nov, and beta-adjusted net leverage of fundamental long-short funds fell to 48.2%, a five-year low. JPMorgan data reported by Reuters showed hedge funds lost more than 3% that week, their worst since April 2025. On 23 Nov the S&P 500 rose 4.73% to 7,237.17 and the Nasdaq Composite 6.51%, while the VIX fell about 26% to 26.62. Goldman had estimated trend-following funds would still sell about $28.6bn of stocks this week even if markets rose.
stories.market: Low net leverage and heavy single-stock shorts make the rebound vulnerable to short covering in crowded tech names; CTA models remain net short about $19bn of US equities, so systematic selling has not yet turned to buying.

body: Goldman's prime desk said funds sold 1.5 shares short for every share bought in the week to 20 Nov, the third straight week of net selling of global stocks. Net exposure of long/short funds fell to the lowest since before the pandemic.

Morgan Stanley put US long/short net leverage at 41%, down five points in a week; the troughs in 2020 and April 2025 were 30-35%. In the week to 6 Nov, gross leverage fell 8.7 points to 207.5%, the largest drop since March 2020.

Goldman estimated trend-following funds had sold about $57bn of equities over the past month, leaving them net short about $19bn. Its models projected further selling this week of about $28.6bn if stocks rose, $65.8bn if flat and $80.6bn if they fell.
Monday's rebound, led by Nvidia's 31.5% surge, lifted the Dow 3.01% to 49,595.31 and the Russell 2000 3.40%, and came after funds had cut exposure to multi-year lows.

stories.headline: Toronto Snaps a Seven-Session Losing Streak With Its Biggest Gain Since April 2025
stories.summary: The S&P/TSX Composite jumped 2.69% to 34,081.44 on Monday 23 Nov, ending a seven-session slide that had taken it to a six-month low, with base metals and technology leading (MarketScreener/MT Newswires). The index is still down 4.59% over five sessions but up 7.47% for the year.
stories.market: Gold and copper names led: Montage Gold +12.46%, NovaGold +12.01% and Capstone Copper +8.36% on 23 Nov, while Telus fell 4.85%.

body: Canada's main index closed at 34,081.44 on 23 Nov, a gain of 2.69% and its largest one-day advance since April 2025, according to MT Newswires via MarketScreener. The move broke a seven-session losing streak that had pushed the benchmark to a six-month low.

Base-metal and technology stocks led, echoing the rebound in US chip shares. Keel Infrastructure rose 16.36%, Montage Gold 12.46% and NovaGold Resources 12.01%. Telus was among the biggest decliners, down 4.85%.
Domestic data have been soft: Statistics Canada said on 20 Nov that September retail sales rose 0.8% but a preliminary estimate points to a 1.5% drop in October.

timeline.text: StatCan flags a 1.5% October retail-sales drop; TSX extends losing streak to seven sessions.
TSX rises 2.69% to 34,081.44, biggest gain since April 2025.

stories.headline: Brazil's Lower House Passes the Fiscal Bill 353-128 While Cheaper Oil Pushes the Ibovespa to a Six-Month Low
stories.summary: The Chamber of Deputies approved the main text of the Senate-passed fiscal bill PLP 299/2026 by 353 votes to 128 late on 23 Nov, unchanged from the Senate version, so it can go to President Lula once separate amendments are dealt with (TMC). The Senate rapporteur estimates up to R$56.1bn of extra revenue in 2027; the bill trims the real spending-growth cap to 2% in years with budget freezes and cuts tax breaks across the board.
stories.market: The Ibovespa fell 0.95% to 164,796 on 23 Nov, its lowest close in at least six months, as Petrobras dropped 3.21% with Brent; the real firmed 0.31% to R$5.9306 per dollar (Rio Times). The vote came after the close.

body: In an extraordinary session on the night of 23 Nov, Brazil's Chamber of Deputies approved the base text of PLP 299/2026 by 353 to 128, well above the 257 votes needed. Rapporteur Mauro Benevides Filho rejected all amendments, so the text matches the Senate's and does not return there; once remaining motions are voted it goes to President Lula for signature.

The bill lowers the cap on real federal spending growth from 2.5% to 2% in years when spending freezes apply, widens the executive's power to freeze discretionary outlays, imposes a linear cut to sector tax breaks and lets the tax authority temporarily limit offsetting of tax credits. Senate rapporteur Eduardo Braga puts the potential 2027 revenue gain at up to R$56.1bn. Part of the road-diesel subsidy tied to the Middle East conflict is excluded from the 2026 target.

Markets traded before the vote. The Ibovespa lost 0.95% to 164,796, a third straight fall and 21.2% below its 9 Oct high of 209,067. Petrobras preferred shares fell 3.21% to R$41.30 as Brent fell about 3%, despite a newly approved US$122bn investment plan to 2031. The real gained slightly, closing at R$5.9306 per dollar.

stories.headline: Mexico's GDP Beats Forecasts and the IPC Ends a Six-Day Slide, but the Peso Holds Near a One-Year Low
stories.summary: Mexico's third-quarter GDP grew 3.3% year on year and 0.9% quarter on quarter, above forecasts of 3.1% and 0.8%, while September economic activity rose 3.0% on the year (Rio Times, 23 Nov). The S&P/BMV IPC rose 1.26% to 69,490.83, ending a six-session losing streak.
stories.market: The peso was little changed at 19.1775 per dollar on 23 Nov, which Rio Times calls its weakest in at least 12 months; Banxico's 5 Nov cut to 6.25% has narrowed the carry advantage.

body: Third-quarter GDP data showed growth of 3.3% year on year, against 3.1% expected and 2.2% in the prior quarter, and 0.9% quarter on quarter. September's economic-activity index rose 3.0% on the year but fell 0.7% on the month.
The IPC closed at 69,490.83, up 1.26%, snapping six straight losses and sitting about 3.5% below its 11 Nov 12-month high of 72,006. The rebound tracked Wall Street's surge.
The peso stayed weak at 19.1775 per dollar. Banxico cut its benchmark rate to 6.25% on 5 Nov in a 3-2 vote.

stories.headline: Argentine Risk Premium Falls 4% to 1,027 as ADRs Rally During the Buenos Aires Holiday
stories.summary: JPMorgan's country-risk index for Argentina fell 43 points to 1,027 basis points on Monday 23 Nov, still above 1,000 after a 29% November rise, as sovereign bonds rebounded in New York (El Esquiú/Noticias Argentinas). Local markets were shut for National Sovereignty Day, so the Merval and peso trade again on Tuesday.
stories.market: Argentine ADRs rose up to 5.4% in New York on 23 Nov, led by Galicia and BBVA Argentina, with Globant +5.3%, Central Puerto +5.2% and MercadoLibre +5.0%.

body: Argentina's sovereign spread narrowed to 1,027 basis points on 23 Nov from 1,070 on Friday, according to JPMorgan's EMBI measure cited by Noticias Argentinas. The index is still up 29% in November after hitting its highest level since the 2025 elections.
With Buenos Aires closed for the Día de la Soberanía holiday, the move came entirely in New York-traded assets, where bank ADRs climbed as much as 5.4% alongside the global risk rebound.
The test for local prices comes on Tuesday 24 Nov, when the Merval and the official and parallel dollar markets reopen after the government ruled out a devaluation over the weekend.
